Internal playbook · Founder review required

Version 0.1 / 28 October 2026

Make the mechanism clear.
Make the judgment yours.

A weekly research publication for novice investors and finance students learning how macro developments connect to US and European equity indices.

Working proposal, not an operating track record. Publication cadence, individual responsibilities, pricing and the founder’s viewpoint remain decisions to approve. The historical pilot demonstrates the format; it does not prove willingness to pay or investing skill.

Why this pilot uses June 2024

The archived June 2024 releases offer a bounded, reproducible case of policy divergence, with inflation and growth evidence available at the time. This makes the editorial method reviewable without presenting unverified October 2026 news or prices. A live weekly edition still requires a fresh cutoff, verified current releases and calendars, permitted market data, and the founder’s approved interpretation. The pilot makes no claim to be current research.

The editorial contract

Each issue answers one question: what changed, why could it matter for equity indices, and what evidence would change our interpretation? Explain the economic transmission before offering a view. The paid product should earn attention through reliable selection, transparent reasoning and learning value. Do not sell a promise of superior returns.

Two reading depths

Five-minute issue: one-sentence thesis, three-item overview, one dominant theme, US–Europe comparison, one explained concept, conditional scenarios and a small watchlist. Target 1,000–1,400 words excluding detailed internal records; monitor actual reading time with pilot readers.

Research trail: source notes, data vintage, units, formula notes and the correction record. Keep deeper evidence available without forcing beginners through every calculation.

Useful specificity

Explain a new term at first use. Separate a rate from a change in a rate; a percentage from percentage points; disinflation from falling prices; quarterly growth from annualised growth.

Use “could” where the channel is conditional. State what is missing. A narrow conclusion backed by evidence is more useful than a strong conclusion borrowed from a headline.

The repeatable weekly research loop

  1. Set the information cutoff. Record date, time and timezone. Save the exact release, retrieval date, reference period and whether it is preliminary, revised or final. Keep release-day data separate from later revised series.
  2. Build a small evidence ledger. Capture each factual claim, primary source URL, exact table or paragraph, units and release time. Prioritise changes that alter an existing thesis rather than summarising every headline.
  3. Choose one dominant question. Write a tentative thesis and the strongest plausible opposing explanation. If no coherent thesis survives, publish an honest explanation of uncertainty.
  4. Trace the mechanism. Data → expected policy and financing conditions → demand, margins and earnings → valuation → index composition and investor currency. Mark each inferential link. Avoid jumping straight from GDP to “stocks up.”
  5. Align the comparison. Match dates, frequency, currency, dividends and geography. For an equity return, name the exact index variant, closing observations, price/total return status, calculation and source licence. An ETF return is not automatically the index return.
  6. Draft for beginners. Write the overview last so it matches the argument. Include a visual only if it sharpens the question and can be reproduced from the ledger.
  7. Challenge and check. Recompute calculations independently; read the original source beside every number. Ask whether a policy move was expected before calling it a market surprise. Without consensus or pricing evidence, omit that claim.
  8. Founder edits and signs. The founder selects the thesis, revises the judgment, accepts the counterargument and signs the fact-check sheet. Publish only the approved version. Archive its sources and log substantive corrections visibly.
  9. Learn after publication. Record reader confusion and later disconfirming evidence. Update the thesis on evidence rather than rewriting the old issue to appear prescient.

Primary source desk

SourceUseEditorial caution
Federal ReserveStatements, implementation notes, projections, minutes and calendarsDifferentiate announcement, effective date and meeting minutes; projections are conditional, not promises.
ECBPolicy decisions, staff forecasts, press conferences and accountsSpecify deposit, refinancing or lending rate. Euro area does not mean all Europe.
BLSCPI, employment and wagesSeparate seasonal adjustment, monthly/annual changes, surveys and revisions.
BEAGDP, PCE inflation, income and corporate profitsKeep advance/second/third vintages. BEA profits are not index earnings per share.
EurostatHICP, GDP, employment and official release datesFlash estimates can change. Match EU/euro-area geography and country composition.
S&P DJI / STOXXBenchmark definitions, methodology, index variants and licensed observationsRecord exact variant, currency and date. A dynamic page is not a historical factsheet. Check redistribution rights before publishing market data.
Company investor relations / regulatory filingsPublished guidance, margins, geographic sales and financing exposureDistinguish management expectations from realised results. Index attribution requires point-in-time weights.

Six proposed issues

A sequence to test with readers. These are editorial questions, not forecasts or dates for future events.

IssueQuestionConcept and evidence
00 · PilotWhy is a rate cut not a stock-market signal?Discount rates; June 2024 ECB/Fed divergence. Completed historical draft.
01Why can falling inflation leave prices feeling high?Level vs rate of change; CPI/HICP composition and household baskets.
02Can GDP grow while an equity index struggles?Domestic output vs global corporate earnings; matched geographic data.
03Why does a US stock return change for a euro investor?Currency conversion, compounding and hedging; licensed matched observations.
04Does a good data release have to lift markets?Expectations vs outcomes; use a properly sourced consensus or omit “surprise.”
05What does index concentration hide?Market-cap weighting, earnings breadth and historical constituent weights.

ResponsibilityAssigned personRequired evidence

Source and calculation check[Reviewer’s name — assign]Claim ledger, recalculation and resolved discrepancies
Copy and production[Name — assign; may be founder]Language, accessibility, mobile and link checks

If the founder works alone, perform a separate check pass after drafting and label it self-reviewed. Do not imply independent editorial review. Portfolio evidence should show the founder’s real revisions, source choices and rejected explanations—not claim AI-generated drafts as independently authored research.

Pre-publication fact-check sheet

  • Every factual market or macro claim resolves to a primary release or permitted data source.
  • Release date, reference period, retrieval date and information cutoff are recorded.
  • No later data or outcomes leak into a historical reconstruction.
  • Units, adjustment, annualisation, geography and revision vintage agree with the text.
  • Each chart is reproducible; axes, legend, source and observation window are visible.
  • Index comparisons match currency, dividends, close times and period; licences allow use.
  • Observation, inference, hypothetical scenario and unknown are distinguishable.
  • A causal market explanation has evidence beyond events occurring on the same day.
  • Calendar dates and timezones are rechecked immediately before a live issue is sent.
  • There is a credible counterargument and a clear condition that changes the view.
  • No invented expertise, testimonials, subscriber metrics, investment performance or return promises.
  • Founder reviewed every claim and recorded approval; all ownership placeholders are resolved.

Honest AI usage record

28 October 2026 — prototype production. An OpenAI Codex agent selected the historical June 2024 episode, searched and read official releases, drafted both documents, calculated the approximate GDP conversion and coded the original SVG chart. It also wrote the source-data JSON and production scripts. No individual founder analysis or approval is claimed.

Checks performed: official release vintages cross-checked against each quoted macro observation; chart values matched BLS Table A; quarterly GDP conversion recorded; historical watch dates traced to contemporaneous release notices. Structural index descriptions retrieved in 2026 are disclosed separately. Layout and data checks are recorded in the delivery verification report.

Limits: this issue contains no validated market-return series, consensus expectations, sector attribution or reader-testing results. The pilot is therefore a macro teaching case, not an assessment of realised index performance. No suitable writing reference was obtained; an English editorial house voice was drafted for founder review.

Founder must add: source-by-source approval, personal thesis revisions, accepted/rejected AI suggestions, reviewer identity and publication decision. Preserve the original draft alongside edits so the portfolio accurately shows what the founder contributed.

Suggested reader disclosure

“AI tools assisted with research organisation, drafting and chart production. [Author name] selected the final argument, checked the cited facts and calculations, and is responsible for the published analysis.”

Use this wording only after those author actions actually occur. Until then, retain the working-draft disclosure used in the pilot.

EVADE RESEARCH · EDITORIAL PLAYBOOK v0.1
Prepared 28 October 2026 · Internal working document · No cloud publication or message sending performed.

Find the story. Check the release. Explain the mechanism.

Evade Research is being developed as a weekly macro briefing for newer investors, supported by one or two short Market Notes each week. Notes explain one useful mechanism with a worked example, a clear limitation and links to the evidence.

The proposed research desk combines Bloomberg’s reporting, FinancialJuice’s event monitoring and TradingView’s charts and company data. Primary releases and company filings anchor factual verification. The aim is to show how an interpretation was built, and what could change it.

This is a proposed workflow. No connected accounts, live feeds, publishing automation or data redistribution rights are claimed.

Bloomberg · Context and reporting

Use reporting to identify the wider story, compare explanations and trace original documents. Bloomberg documents custom news and alerts within its Terminal product; that does not establish Terminal access here. Bloomberg Professional Services

Some newsletters are free; subscriber-only newsletters require eligible subscriptions. Bloomberg Help Center

Read through access the founder actually holds. Record the article’s publication time and link; distinguish reported facts from the publication’s analysis. A Bloomberg.com article or newsletter is not evidence of a Terminal entitlement.

FinancialJuice · News and event triage

Use categorised headlines, the calendar and available alerts to identify events worth investigating. Its PRO page advertises real-time text, voice, calendar and browser alerts. The public page also displays a delayed-voice label. FinancialJuice · FinancialJuice

Exact free-feed delay and account-specific delivery latency were not established from accessible official documentation. Do not publish a numerical delay claim or promise instant notification. Check the displayed timestamp, timezone, connection status and actual entitlement before relying on a feed. Some features require registration; no account was configured or tested here. FinancialJuice

TradingView · Charting and company financials

Use charts to inspect a defined instrument and period, and financials to compare income statements, balance sheets, cash flows and ratios. Company financials can be viewed across reporting periods; availability and capacity depend on the instrument and plan. TradingView · TradingView

Check the symbol, exchange, currency, adjustment and data-status label. A paid charting plan does not automatically include every exchange’s real-time feed. Company data can differ from original reports, so verify key figures against filings. TradingView

Verify the underlying evidence

For a macro number, open the central bank or statistical agency’s release and record the reference period, release time, units and revision vintage. For a company figure, check the issuer’s report or regulatory filing and whether the number is annual, quarterly, trailing, reported or adjusted. A fast headline is a prompt to check, not final verification.

Separate the observation from the interpretation and the unknown. A market move occurring after a headline does not by itself prove causation. Label illustrative calculations and retain the inputs and formula.

Access and reuse

Use only public material and subscriptions the founder is authorised to access. Link to reporting; write original explanations. Do not reproduce protected articles, feeds, screenshots or charts on the assumption that a personal subscription permits redistribution. FinancialJuice’s terms specifically restrict copying and aggregation without permission. FinancialJuice

The site does not claim a partnership with these platforms, an account connection or licensed live data. No accounts, alerts, purchases or automatic publication were set up during this research. Platform features and entitlements should be rechecked before adopting the workflow.

Market Notes: the first four weeks

Two possible notes per week; reduce to one when evidence or review time requires it. 400–600 words, one reader question, one worked example or original diagram, one limitation, primary-source links and founder review. No personalised recommendation, live-news requirement or return promise.

  1. Week 1: Why bond prices fall when yields rise; Falling inflation does not necessarily mean falling prices.
  2. Week 2: A policy rate is not the whole yield curve; Why an expected announcement may barely move a market.
  3. Week 3: GDP growth is not the same as index earnings growth; Price return, total return and a euro investor’s currency effect.
  4. Week 4: A company can grow revenue while margins fall; An index can rise while many constituents fall.

Planning only. No automatic publication schedule has been created.
